newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - EU tax policies to come into sharper focus under EMU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU tax policies to come into sharper focus under EMU.

text.p: A credible single European currency could drive participating governments towards common tax policies, a step that would bolster the effectiveness of a single market, experts say.
The economic logic behind such a development, that there are enormous gains to be had from coordinating economic and financial policies, is no doubt controversial.

Critics argue that common tax policies would remove opportunities for governments to promote themselves to businesses and labour while nationalists worry about the loss of sovereignty and an acceleration towards a European super state.

Still, a growing number of observers believe the competitive pressures of monetary union will quickly chip away at differences in national tax rates and simplify the debt financing activities of governments.
The tax issue has already been raised by EU finance ministers who worry about unfair competition between countries joining a single currency, due to start in 1999.
At a recent meeting in Brussels, ministers focused on the broad range of corporate tax rates which encourage companies to play off countries against each other.
While there is no official plan to streamline taxes -- apart from continuing attempts to harmonise indirect taxes, such as VAT -- experts say the real issue is what makes economic sense.
MARKET PRESSURES TO DICTATE TREND
Those forecasting a single tax regime invariably put forward the following argument.

If under monetary union you have a single currency and monetary policy, and rules which effectively constrain budget policies, is it not reasonable to assume that a common form of taxation and public borrowing will quickly follow.
"A common currency will lead to harmonisation faster than people expect," says Anthony Hughes, international tax partner at Coopers & Lybrand in London.
"I think that once we have six states in the euro I can't see why between themselves they would not agree to harmonise their tax base," he added.
The one area where most agree that harmonisation is needed, and likely to appear quickly, is in taxation of interest income.
"Some aspects of the tax system, particularly on capital income, will come more into focus when we have a single currency," noted Neils Thygesen, economist at Copenhagen University.
Luxembourg, for example, has benefited enormously as a tax haven for individuals with high incomes, particularly those in neighbouring Germany.
The EU's smallest country offers no tax on interest, dividends or capital gains, and is estimated to handle about five percent of German banking operations.
The amount of income siphoned off to Luxembourg from Germany has caused dismay among German tax authorities, struggling to save every pfennig they can to meet the Maastricht treaty's budget targets.
EMU CORE COULD EMBRACE SIMILAR TAX REGIME
Legally, experts say there is nothing to prevent a core bloc of countries inside economic and monetary union (EMU) embracing similar tax policies.

While the EU would undoubtedly prefer to reach agreement on taxation among all 15 countries, in practice the path towards a common regime is likely to be more fractured, with a core group inside EMU leading the way.
Nearly all agree that the current requirement of unanimity in EU decision-making has blocked the possiblity of agreement on indirect taxation measures.
"At the end of the day there are going to have to be economic policies which are more in line with one another," said David Evans, European senior tax manager at KPMG in London.
"It seems to me to be a very small step to say there is going to be convergence on taxes as well."
Sceptics of such a scenario say that tax policies are likely to be fiercely guarded by national governments, essentially their last source of expression in economic policy-making.
Moreover, the trend in recent years has been towards greater disparity and higher rates of taxation, particularly in the big revenue-raising areas of income and social contributions.
Astrid Pieron, tax partner at Arthur Anderson in Brussels, says, "In each country the trend is towards increasing taxes."
DATA SHOW TASK WILL BE TOUGH
Recent data from Eurostat, the EU's statistical office, highlight the tough task ahead.

Based on 1995 figures, the average rate of taxes and social contributions as a percentage of GDP stood at 41.7 percent, matching the record level seen in 1993. But around this average differences were quite wide, with Spain at 34.8 percent and Sweden on top at 51.5 percent.

A closer look at the figures, however, shows that for the core group of countries considered most likely to join EMU in 1999 -- Germany, France, Austria and the Benelux countries -- the differences narrow considerably.
Analysts also note that Germany's recent plans to reduce corporate tax rates is partly a recognition of the harm its previous policies have done to employment growth.
Many German firms have relocated their operations outside the country to take advantage of less oppressive tax policies and, of course, cheaper labour.

Finally, much of the EU's relatively high rate of taxation can be explained by generous social and welfare systems which are now under threat because of the need to bring deficits in line with Maastricht.

More fundamentally, economists say such policies are in desperate need of review even without EMU. If Europe ever hopes to create a more vibrant single market, one that generates a high rate of employment, a new approach to taxation will be an important ingredient.
